Recall questions

A1 · State a fact, a name or a learnt reason

A1
State a fact, a name or a learnt reason
Recall · 32 parts · 38 marks in 15 questions
How to spot it

'State', 'Name', 'Give', 'Which of the substances in the list…', or a short 'Explain why' with a standard one-line answer. One or two marks; the answer comes from knowledge, not from the data given.

Common slip

Writing 'iron' when 'iron(III) oxide' is wanted, or listing two answers to hedge.

Technique: Read · Recall · Record
  1. Read. Underline exactly what is asked for: a substance, a use, a colour, a condition, a gas.
  2. Recall. Bring up the fact or the learnt reason from the syllabus.
  3. Record. Give one precise answer, by name or formula. A second, wrong answer cancels a right one.
No questions match the current filters.

Recall questions

A2 · Define a term

A2
Define a term
Recall · 4 parts · 7 marks in 3 questions
How to spot it

'What is meant by…', 'Define…', 'Explain the term…'.

Common slip

Giving half a definition: 'same number of protons' alone scores nothing for isotopes.

Technique: Identify · Include · Illustrate
  1. Identify. Find the key term and the syllabus learning outcome it comes from.
  2. Include. Write the definition with every part, e.g. isotopes: same number of protons AND different numbers of neutrons.
  3. Illustrate. Add an example only if the question asks for one.

Explain questions

B1 · Explain a property from structure and bonding

B1
Explain a property from structure and bonding
Explain · 16 parts · 36 marks in 13 questions
How to spot it

'Explain why X has a high melting point / conducts / is hard / is a gas'; 'Use ideas about structure and bonding'.

Common slip

Writing 'strong bonds' for a simple molecular substance, or 'ions move' for a metal.

Technique: Structure · Species · Strength · Spend
  1. Structure. Name the structure: giant ionic, giant covalent, giant metallic or simple molecular.
  2. Species. Name the particles: ions, atoms, molecules, delocalised electrons.
  3. Strength. Name the force and say whether it is strong or weak: electrostatic attraction, covalent bonds, intermolecular forces.
  4. Spend. State that much (or little) energy is needed to overcome it. For conductivity, name the mobile charge carriers and when they are free to move.
No questions match the current filters.
2025 Paper 2Question 1 Section A · Metallic and ionic structures; graphite6 marks

The arrangement of particles in a solid metal and a solid ionic compound are shown in Fig. 1.1.

(b)

Explain why ionic compounds have high melting points.

2025 · Q1(b)[2]
Ionic compounds have a giant lattice of oppositely charged ions.
There are strong electrostatic forces of attraction between the ions,
so a large amount of energy is needed to overcome them.
[1] strong electrostatic attraction between oppositely charged ions
[1] large amount of (heat) energy needed to overcome these forces
Do not accept 'strong bonds between molecules' or 'intermolecular forces'.
(c)

Compare the electrical conductivity of a metal and an ionic compound.

Use ideas about structure in your answer.

2025 · Q1(c)[3]
A metal conducts electricity in both the solid and molten states,
because its delocalised electrons are free to move and carry charge.
A solid ionic compound does not conduct: its ions are held in fixed
positions in the lattice. It conducts only when molten or in aqueous
solution, when the ions are free to move.
[1] metal conducts (solid and molten) due to mobile delocalised electrons
[1] solid ionic compound does not conduct as ions are in fixed positions
[1] ionic compound conducts when molten / aqueous as ions are mobile
Ionic compounds conduct by moving ions, never by moving electrons.
(d)(ii)

Explain, using Fig. 1.2, how this non-metal conducts electricity.

2025 · Q1(d)(ii)[1]
Each carbon atom is covalently bonded to only three other carbon atoms,
so one outer electron per atom is delocalised and free to move along
the layers, carrying charge.
[1] each C bonded to 3 others so one delocalised electron per C atom moves along the layers
Other parts of this question: (a) E4, (d)(i) F2

2022 Paper 2Question 7 Section B · Types of poly(ethene): LDPE, LLDPE, HDPE and co-polymers2 marks

Poly(ethene)

Types of poly(ethene)

The polymerisation of ethene to make poly(ethene) is usually represented as a simple addition polymerisation reaction which produces a linear chain of carbon and hydrogen atoms as shown in Fig. 7.1.

However, this is a simplified structure. In industry, different processes are used to manufacture several types of poly(ethene), each with a different structure. Fig. 7.2 shows the structures of three types of poly(ethene).

Fig. 7.3 shows another way of representing the polymer chains in each type of poly(ethene). The polymer chains shown in Fig. 7.3 are simplified representations of the real structures.

The carbon atom chains that branch out from the main polymer chain are known as side chains.

Polymerising ethene using heat and pressure results in low-density poly(ethene) (LDPE), a branched polymer. Each single LDPE molecule contains between 4000 and 40000 carbon atoms.

Co-polymers

A co-polymer is polymer that is formed from two (or more) different types of monomer.

LLDPE is made by mixing other alkenes with ethene before polymerisation. This introduces short side chains into the main polymer chain.

For example, ethene molecules can react with butene molecules to form a co-polymer. Three molecules which join to form part of a co-polymer are shown in Fig. 7.4.

The co-polymer produced has a -CH2-CH3 side chain.

World production, uses and properties of different types of poly(ethene)

Side chains push the polymer chains away from each other. In general, polymer chains with fewer side chains can be arranged closer together. This means that polymers with fewer side chains are usually more dense, less flexible, stronger and harder. The world production of each polymer differs because some types of polymer are more useful than others to make products such as building materials, packaging and hot drinks containers.

2024 Paper 2Question 7 Section A · Improving fuels: hydrodesulfurisation, catalytic reforming, flue gas desulfurisation2 marks

Improving Fuels

Sulfur in Crude Oil

Crude oil is separated into fractions which are further processed to make petrol and diesel fuels. Some compounds in the fractions contain sulfur. Removing the sulfur produces ultra-low sulfur petrol and diesel which produce fewer pollutants when they burn.

Hydrodesulfurisation

The sulfur is removed in a process called hydrodesulfurisation. In this process, the compounds that contain sulfur react with hydrogen. The products of the main reaction are a new carbon compound and hydrogen sulfide. The general equation for this process is shown in Equation 1.

Equation 1 R-SH + H2 → R-H + H2S (R = CnH(2n+1))

Catalytic Reforming

Some crude oil fractions are used as a feedstock for a catalytic reforming process. This process produces branched molecules or cyclic molecules from straight chain molecules. The branched molecules burn more smoothly and so are used to improve petrol. Equations 2 and 3 show examples of catalytic reforming reactions.

The catalytic reforming process involves passing heated molecules over a platinum catalyst. Sulfur compounds in the feedstock bind to the catalyst surface and make the reactions less effective. This is why hydrodesulfurisation is used to remove as much sulfur as possible from the compounds.

Flue Gas Desulfurisation

Coal and natural gas also contain sulfur compounds. The sulfur dioxide produced during combustion of these fuels in power stations is removed from the waste gases by flue gas desulfurisation. The sulfur dioxide is treated with powdered limestone. Limestone is mostly calcium carbonate with small amounts of impurities. The purity of limestone used in flue gas desulfurisation is 98%.

The reaction that takes place during the process is shown in Equation 4.

Equation 4 SO2(g) + CaCO3(s) → CaSO3(s) + CO2(g)

Nitrogen dioxide is another gas produced during combustion. Nitrogen dioxide is also removed from the waste gases by reaction with calcium carbonate in limestone. The products of the reaction between calcium carbonate and nitrogen dioxide are shown in Table 7.1.

Table 7.1
gas removedproducts of reaction with calcium carbonate
nitrogen dioxideCO2, Ca(NO3)2, Ca(NO2)2
(c)(i)

so fewer reactant molecules can be adsorbed / react there;
the rate of reforming falls (the catalyst is poisoned).
[1] sulfur compounds block / occupy the surface (active sites) of the platinum
[1] fewer reactant molecules adsorbed, so slower reaction / less product formed
Other parts of this question: (a)(i) F2, (a)(ii) B7, (b)(i) C1, (b)(ii) D1, (c)(ii) E2

The number of outer (valence) electrons increases from 1 to 8 across the period,
and the nuclear charge increases, so outer electrons are held more strongly.
Li and Be have few outer electrons, which they lose to form
positive ions (metallic behaviour).
N, O and F have 5 to 7 outer electrons and gain or share electrons to complete
their outer shells, forming negative ions or covalent bonds (non-metallic).
[1] number of outer / valence electrons increases across the period
[1] elements on the left lose electrons to form positive ions (metallic)
[1] elements on the right gain or share electrons to form negative ions / covalent bonds (non-metallic)
Neon has a full outer shell and does not form compounds.

2025 Paper 2Question 7 Section A · Carbon capture storage (CCS) from methane-fuelled power stations3 marks

Carbon capture storage (CCS)

Some power stations that generate electricity use methane as a fuel. Carbon capture storage (CCS) reduces the amount of carbon dioxide entering the atmosphere. This is done by capturing carbon from methane in the form of carbon dioxide. Carbon from methane can be captured either before the methane burns (pre-combustion) or after combustion (post-combustion) as carbon dioxide.

Carbon dioxide can be stored deep underground in the space left when crude oil is extracted.

Pre-combustion capture

Steam methane reforming (SMR) and water-gas shift (WGS) are two reactions involved in pre-combustion capture of carbon from methane.

In SMR, steam reacts with methane at a pressure of 3–25 atmospheres and at a temperature of 700–1000 °C.

SMR reaction equation:

CH4 + H2O ⇌ CO + 3H2 ΔH = +206 kJ/mol

The SMR reaction is reversible and therefore the products contain small amounts of unreacted methane and water. The reaction has a percentage yield of 74%.

This is followed by the WGS reaction at 200–400 °C using a catalyst.

WGS reaction equation:

CO + H2O ⇌ CO2 + H2 ΔH = –41 kJ/mol

The carbon dioxide produced in the WGS reaction is separated from hydrogen and goes to be stored. The hydrogen is burned as a fuel to generate electricity. It does not cause environmental harm when it is combusted.

Post-combustion capture

Some power stations capture the carbon dioxide post-combustion. In order to easily separate the carbon dioxide after the reaction, the methane is burned in pure oxygen rather than air.

CH4 + 2O2 → CO2 + 2H2O

The water vapour that is produced is separated from the mixture of products. The carbon dioxide then goes to be stored.

Storing carbon dioxide

The carbon dioxide collected from the power station is pressurised. This produces liquid carbon dioxide which can then be pumped directly to be stored deep underground.

The fuel industry thinks that the space made available from the extraction of crude oil will be enough to store all the carbon dioxide produced in the world from fossil fuel combustion for many years.

2023 Paper 2Question 7 Section B · Comparing vehicle fuels (ethanol, LPG, LNG, petrol)2 marks

Comparing vehicle fuels

Car manufacturers make cars which use a range of different fuels. Some fuels are renewable, which means that they do not rely on using finite resources such as fossil fuels, and some are 'carbon neutral', which means that their use does not lead to an overall increase in the amount of carbon in the atmosphere. Other factors that need to be taken into account are the energy output of the fuel and how easy it is to store in the vehicle.

Ethanol in fuels

Ethanol fuel contains 93–96% ethanol. It is used mainly in countries such as Brazil where sugarcane can be grown in large quantities. The percentage of ethanol in the fuel is indicated by the name of the fuel. For example, E25 contains 25% ethanol by mass and E70 contains 70% ethanol by mass. In most other countries, standard petrol contains ethanol as an additive. Typically, standard petrol contains about 10% ethanol by mass and the rest is hydrocarbons. Ethanol is a useful additive to standard petrol because it increases the percentage of oxygen available for combustion.

Producing ethanol

Ethanol for use as a fuel for vehicles can be produced by either fermentation or by the catalytic addition of steam to ethene in an industrial process (see Table 7.1).

Table 7.1
processraw materialsadditional information
fermentationsugar from sugarcanereactions after fermentation produce ethanoic acid and ethyl ethanoate impurities separated by distillation or use of molecular sieves
catalytic addition of steam to etheneethene from cracking of naphtha from petroleumconditions: • 300 °C • 70 atm pressure • phosphoric(V) acid catalyst

Data about energy output

The enthalpy change of combustion is the energy given out when one mole of a pure compound burns. This can be used to compare the energy output of the main compounds in fuels, as shown in Table 7.2.

Table 7.2
type of fuelmain compoundenthalpy change of combustion of main compound in kJ/mol
LNG (liquified natural gas)methane–890
LPG (liquified petroleum gas)butane–2877
petroloctane–5470
ethanol fuelethanol–1366

Fuels are mixtures of compounds and the enthalpy change of combustion does not take into account the state or the density of the fuel.

Comparing fuels

Gaseous fuels take up a lot of storage space in a vehicle, therefore they are compressed into a liquid state. Both the mass density and the energy density (energy released per litre) of the fuels are important because they determine how far the vehicle can travel before needing to be refuelled.

Table 7.3 compares the mass density and energy density of some liquid fuels (1 L = 1000 cm³).

Table 7.3
type of fuelmass density in g/cm³energy density (energy released per litre) in kJ/L
LNG (liquified natural gas)0.4522200
LPG (liquified petroleum gas)0.5526500
petrol0.7534200
ethanol fuel0.7925000

Energy densities of fuels can be approximated by calculations which use the enthalpy change of combustion of the main compound in the fuel and the mass density of the fuel. These calculated values differ from the values shown in Table 7.3 because fuels are actually mixtures of compounds.

One way of comparing fuels is by using a GGE index. This compares the energy output of one litre of petrol to the energy output of one litre of the fuel. So, for example, a fuel with a GGE of 2.0 contains half as much energy per litre as one litre of petrol. Two litres of fuel would need to be carried in the vehicle to give the same energy output as one litre of petrol. This is more useful than looking at enthalpy change of combustion data because it takes into account the volume of fuel that can be stored in the car. Comparing ethanol fuel to petrol gives ethanol fuel a GGE of 1.4.

2024 · Q8(b)(ii)[3]
Electrodes are inert, so nothing is deposited on or removed from them;

2024 Paper 2Question 7 Section A · Improving fuels: hydrodesulfurisation, catalytic reforming, flue gas desulfurisation1 mark

Improving Fuels

Sulfur in Crude Oil

Crude oil is separated into fractions which are further processed to make petrol and diesel fuels. Some compounds in the fractions contain sulfur. Removing the sulfur produces ultra-low sulfur petrol and diesel which produce fewer pollutants when they burn.

Hydrodesulfurisation

The sulfur is removed in a process called hydrodesulfurisation. In this process, the compounds that contain sulfur react with hydrogen. The products of the main reaction are a new carbon compound and hydrogen sulfide. The general equation for this process is shown in Equation 1.

Equation 1 R-SH + H2 → R-H + H2S (R = CnH(2n+1))

Catalytic Reforming

Some crude oil fractions are used as a feedstock for a catalytic reforming process. This process produces branched molecules or cyclic molecules from straight chain molecules. The branched molecules burn more smoothly and so are used to improve petrol. Equations 2 and 3 show examples of catalytic reforming reactions.

The catalytic reforming process involves passing heated molecules over a platinum catalyst. Sulfur compounds in the feedstock bind to the catalyst surface and make the reactions less effective. This is why hydrodesulfurisation is used to remove as much sulfur as possible from the compounds.

Flue Gas Desulfurisation

Coal and natural gas also contain sulfur compounds. The sulfur dioxide produced during combustion of these fuels in power stations is removed from the waste gases by flue gas desulfurisation. The sulfur dioxide is treated with powdered limestone. Limestone is mostly calcium carbonate with small amounts of impurities. The purity of limestone used in flue gas desulfurisation is 98%.

The reaction that takes place during the process is shown in Equation 4.

Equation 4 SO2(g) + CaCO3(s) → CaSO3(s) + CO2(g)

Nitrogen dioxide is another gas produced during combustion. Nitrogen dioxide is also removed from the waste gases by reaction with calcium carbonate in limestone. The products of the reaction between calcium carbonate and nitrogen dioxide are shown in Table 7.1.

Table 7.1
gas removedproducts of reaction with calcium carbonate
nitrogen dioxideCO2, Ca(NO3)2, Ca(NO2)2

The reason must be the increase in oxidation state of H from 0 to +1 (or loss of electrons). Do not accept "hydrogen gains sulfur".

General Equations for Reactions of Acids

Some sources, such as text books and websites, represent the general formula of an acid as HA, where A is an anion. HA can be used to give general equations for the reactions of acids.

For example, the reaction of acids with Group II metal hydroxides may be shown as:

equation 1 2HA + M(OH)2 → MA2 + 2H2O

And the reaction of acids with any metal can be shown as:

equation 2 xHA + M → MAx + (x/2)H2

where x is the value of the positive charge on the metal ion.

(a)(i)

Which acids in Table 6.1 fit the general formula HA and which do not?

Explain your reasoning with reference to the ions present in each acid.

2021 · Q6(a)(i)[2]
Hydrochloric acid and ethanoic acid fit HA: each molecule gives
one H+ ion (HCl → H+ + Cl-; CH3COOH → H+ + CH3COO-).
Sulfuric acid does not: each molecule gives two H+ ions and
SO42- (H2A); [H+] is twice the acid concentration.
[1] HCl and ethanoic acid fit HA: one H+ per molecule, anion Cl- / CH3COO-
[1] sulfuric acid does not: two H+ per molecule with SO42- ion
(b)(ii)

State and explain the factors that affect the pH of an acid using information from Table 6.1.

2021 · Q6(b)(ii)[3]
pH depends on [H+]: the higher [H+], the lower the pH.
Concentration: more concentrated acid gives more H+ (HCl 0.01, pH
2.0; HCl 0.10, pH 1.0).
Strength: HCl is strong, fully ionised; ethanoic acid is weak,
partly ionised, so 0.01 mol/dm³ gives only 0.0004 H+ (pH 3.4).
Basicity: H2SO4 gives 2 H+ per molecule, so 0.01 mol/dm³ gives
0.02 H+ and a lower pH (1.7) than HCl (2.0).
[1] concentration of acid: higher concentration, higher [H+], lower pH
[1] strength: strong acid fully ionised, weak (ethanoic) acid partially ionised, higher pH

B9
Explain an energy change using bonds
Explain · 2 parts · 3 marks in 2 questions
How to spot it

'Explain why the reaction is exothermic', 'why more energy is released', 'why heat is needed to start the reaction'.

Common slip

Saying bond breaking releases energy.

Technique: Break · Build · Balance
  1. Break. Bond breaking absorbs energy; heating supplies the activation energy to start it.
  2. Build. Bond forming releases energy; more or stronger bonds formed release more.
  3. Balance. Compare the two: more released than absorbed means exothermic (ΔH negative).

2025 Paper 2Question 7 Section A · Carbon capture storage (CCS) from methane-fuelled power stations2 marks

Carbon capture storage (CCS)

Some power stations that generate electricity use methane as a fuel. Carbon capture storage (CCS) reduces the amount of carbon dioxide entering the atmosphere. This is done by capturing carbon from methane in the form of carbon dioxide. Carbon from methane can be captured either before the methane burns (pre-combustion) or after combustion (post-combustion) as carbon dioxide.

Carbon dioxide can be stored deep underground in the space left when crude oil is extracted.

Pre-combustion capture

Steam methane reforming (SMR) and water-gas shift (WGS) are two reactions involved in pre-combustion capture of carbon from methane.

In SMR, steam reacts with methane at a pressure of 3–25 atmospheres and at a temperature of 700–1000 °C.

SMR reaction equation:

CH4 + H2O ⇌ CO + 3H2 ΔH = +206 kJ/mol

The SMR reaction is reversible and therefore the products contain small amounts of unreacted methane and water. The reaction has a percentage yield of 74%.

This is followed by the WGS reaction at 200–400 °C using a catalyst.

WGS reaction equation:

CO + H2O ⇌ CO2 + H2 ΔH = –41 kJ/mol

The carbon dioxide produced in the WGS reaction is separated from hydrogen and goes to be stored. The hydrogen is burned as a fuel to generate electricity. It does not cause environmental harm when it is combusted.

Post-combustion capture

Some power stations capture the carbon dioxide post-combustion. In order to easily separate the carbon dioxide after the reaction, the methane is burned in pure oxygen rather than air.

CH4 + 2O2 → CO2 + 2H2O

The water vapour that is produced is separated from the mixture of products. The carbon dioxide then goes to be stored.

Storing carbon dioxide

The carbon dioxide collected from the power station is pressurised. This produces liquid carbon dioxide which can then be pumped directly to be stored deep underground.

The fuel industry thinks that the space made available from the extraction of crude oil will be enough to store all the carbon dioxide produced in the world from fossil fuel combustion for many years.

(e)

Arrangement: the molecules change from being far apart and randomly
arranged to being close together but still randomly arranged.

to moving more slowly, sliding past one another.
[1] arrangement: far apart → close together (still random / disordered)
[1] movement: fast and random in all directions → slower, sliding past each other
Do not accept 'molecules vibrate about fixed positions' (that is a solid).

2024 Paper 2Question 7 Section A · Improving fuels: hydrodesulfurisation, catalytic reforming, flue gas desulfurisation3 marks

Improving Fuels

Sulfur in Crude Oil

Crude oil is separated into fractions which are further processed to make petrol and diesel fuels. Some compounds in the fractions contain sulfur. Removing the sulfur produces ultra-low sulfur petrol and diesel which produce fewer pollutants when they burn.

Hydrodesulfurisation

The sulfur is removed in a process called hydrodesulfurisation. In this process, the compounds that contain sulfur react with hydrogen. The products of the main reaction are a new carbon compound and hydrogen sulfide. The general equation for this process is shown in Equation 1.

Equation 1 R-SH + H2 → R-H + H2S (R = CnH(2n+1))

Catalytic Reforming

Some crude oil fractions are used as a feedstock for a catalytic reforming process. This process produces branched molecules or cyclic molecules from straight chain molecules. The branched molecules burn more smoothly and so are used to improve petrol. Equations 2 and 3 show examples of catalytic reforming reactions.

The catalytic reforming process involves passing heated molecules over a platinum catalyst. Sulfur compounds in the feedstock bind to the catalyst surface and make the reactions less effective. This is why hydrodesulfurisation is used to remove as much sulfur as possible from the compounds.

Flue Gas Desulfurisation

Coal and natural gas also contain sulfur compounds. The sulfur dioxide produced during combustion of these fuels in power stations is removed from the waste gases by flue gas desulfurisation. The sulfur dioxide is treated with powdered limestone. Limestone is mostly calcium carbonate with small amounts of impurities. The purity of limestone used in flue gas desulfurisation is 98%.

The reaction that takes place during the process is shown in Equation 4.

Equation 4 SO2(g) + CaCO3(s) → CaSO3(s) + CO2(g)

Nitrogen dioxide is another gas produced during combustion. Nitrogen dioxide is also removed from the waste gases by reaction with calcium carbonate in limestone. The products of the reaction between calcium carbonate and nitrogen dioxide are shown in Table 7.1.

Table 7.1
gas removedproducts of reaction with calcium carbonate
nitrogen dioxideCO2, Ca(NO3)2, Ca(NO2)2

2022 Paper 2Question 7 Section B · Types of poly(ethene): LDPE, LLDPE, HDPE and co-polymers3 marks

Poly(ethene)

Types of poly(ethene)

The polymerisation of ethene to make poly(ethene) is usually represented as a simple addition polymerisation reaction which produces a linear chain of carbon and hydrogen atoms as shown in Fig. 7.1.

However, this is a simplified structure. In industry, different processes are used to manufacture several types of poly(ethene), each with a different structure. Fig. 7.2 shows the structures of three types of poly(ethene).

Fig. 7.3 shows another way of representing the polymer chains in each type of poly(ethene). The polymer chains shown in Fig. 7.3 are simplified representations of the real structures.

The carbon atom chains that branch out from the main polymer chain are known as side chains.

Polymerising ethene using heat and pressure results in low-density poly(ethene) (LDPE), a branched polymer. Each single LDPE molecule contains between 4000 and 40000 carbon atoms.

Co-polymers

A co-polymer is polymer that is formed from two (or more) different types of monomer.

LLDPE is made by mixing other alkenes with ethene before polymerisation. This introduces short side chains into the main polymer chain.

For example, ethene molecules can react with butene molecules to form a co-polymer. Three molecules which join to form part of a co-polymer are shown in Fig. 7.4.

The co-polymer produced has a -CH2-CH3 side chain.

World production, uses and properties of different types of poly(ethene)

Side chains push the polymer chains away from each other. In general, polymer chains with fewer side chains can be arranged closer together. This means that polymers with fewer side chains are usually more dense, less flexible, stronger and harder. The world production of each polymer differs because some types of polymer are more useful than others to make products such as building materials, packaging and hot drinks containers.

2025 Paper 2Question 7 Section A · Carbon capture storage (CCS) from methane-fuelled power stations3 marks

Carbon capture storage (CCS)

Some power stations that generate electricity use methane as a fuel. Carbon capture storage (CCS) reduces the amount of carbon dioxide entering the atmosphere. This is done by capturing carbon from methane in the form of carbon dioxide. Carbon from methane can be captured either before the methane burns (pre-combustion) or after combustion (post-combustion) as carbon dioxide.

Carbon dioxide can be stored deep underground in the space left when crude oil is extracted.

Pre-combustion capture

Steam methane reforming (SMR) and water-gas shift (WGS) are two reactions involved in pre-combustion capture of carbon from methane.

In SMR, steam reacts with methane at a pressure of 3–25 atmospheres and at a temperature of 700–1000 °C.

SMR reaction equation:

CH4 + H2O ⇌ CO + 3H2 ΔH = +206 kJ/mol

The SMR reaction is reversible and therefore the products contain small amounts of unreacted methane and water. The reaction has a percentage yield of 74%.

This is followed by the WGS reaction at 200–400 °C using a catalyst.

WGS reaction equation:

CO + H2O ⇌ CO2 + H2 ΔH = –41 kJ/mol

The carbon dioxide produced in the WGS reaction is separated from hydrogen and goes to be stored. The hydrogen is burned as a fuel to generate electricity. It does not cause environmental harm when it is combusted.

Post-combustion capture

Some power stations capture the carbon dioxide post-combustion. In order to easily separate the carbon dioxide after the reaction, the methane is burned in pure oxygen rather than air.

CH4 + 2O2 → CO2 + 2H2O

The water vapour that is produced is separated from the mixture of products. The carbon dioxide then goes to be stored.

Storing carbon dioxide

The carbon dioxide collected from the power station is pressurised. This produces liquid carbon dioxide which can then be pumped directly to be stored deep underground.

The fuel industry thinks that the space made available from the extraction of crude oil will be enough to store all the carbon dioxide produced in the world from fossil fuel combustion for many years.

(1 tonne = 106 g)

actual mass = 74/100 x 375 000 = 277 500 g
= 2.78 x 105 g (3 s.f.)
mass of hydrogen = 278 000 g (2.78 x 105 g, 0.278 tonne)
[1] n(CH4) = 62 500 mol
[1] theoretical mass H2 = 3 x 62 500 x 2 = 375 000 g

Accept 277 500 g. Common error: forgetting the 74% yield (375 000 g).

2023 Paper 2Question 7 Section B · Comparing vehicle fuels (ethanol, LPG, LNG, petrol)2 marks

Comparing vehicle fuels

Car manufacturers make cars which use a range of different fuels. Some fuels are renewable, which means that they do not rely on using finite resources such as fossil fuels, and some are 'carbon neutral', which means that their use does not lead to an overall increase in the amount of carbon in the atmosphere. Other factors that need to be taken into account are the energy output of the fuel and how easy it is to store in the vehicle.

Ethanol in fuels

Ethanol fuel contains 93–96% ethanol. It is used mainly in countries such as Brazil where sugarcane can be grown in large quantities. The percentage of ethanol in the fuel is indicated by the name of the fuel. For example, E25 contains 25% ethanol by mass and E70 contains 70% ethanol by mass. In most other countries, standard petrol contains ethanol as an additive. Typically, standard petrol contains about 10% ethanol by mass and the rest is hydrocarbons. Ethanol is a useful additive to standard petrol because it increases the percentage of oxygen available for combustion.

Producing ethanol

Ethanol for use as a fuel for vehicles can be produced by either fermentation or by the catalytic addition of steam to ethene in an industrial process (see Table 7.1).

Table 7.1
processraw materialsadditional information
fermentationsugar from sugarcanereactions after fermentation produce ethanoic acid and ethyl ethanoate impurities separated by distillation or use of molecular sieves
catalytic addition of steam to etheneethene from cracking of naphtha from petroleumconditions: • 300 °C • 70 atm pressure • phosphoric(V) acid catalyst

Data about energy output

The enthalpy change of combustion is the energy given out when one mole of a pure compound burns. This can be used to compare the energy output of the main compounds in fuels, as shown in Table 7.2.

Table 7.2
type of fuelmain compoundenthalpy change of combustion of main compound in kJ/mol
LNG (liquified natural gas)methane–890
LPG (liquified petroleum gas)butane–2877
petroloctane–5470
ethanol fuelethanol–1366

Fuels are mixtures of compounds and the enthalpy change of combustion does not take into account the state or the density of the fuel.

Comparing fuels

Gaseous fuels take up a lot of storage space in a vehicle, therefore they are compressed into a liquid state. Both the mass density and the energy density (energy released per litre) of the fuels are important because they determine how far the vehicle can travel before needing to be refuelled.

Table 7.3 compares the mass density and energy density of some liquid fuels (1 L = 1000 cm³).

Table 7.3
type of fuelmass density in g/cm³energy density (energy released per litre) in kJ/L
LNG (liquified natural gas)0.4522200
LPG (liquified petroleum gas)0.5526500
petrol0.7534200
ethanol fuel0.7925000

Energy densities of fuels can be approximated by calculations which use the enthalpy change of combustion of the main compound in the fuel and the mass density of the fuel. These calculated values differ from the values shown in Table 7.3 because fuels are actually mixtures of compounds.

One way of comparing fuels is by using a GGE index. This compares the energy output of one litre of petrol to the energy output of one litre of the fuel. So, for example, a fuel with a GGE of 2.0 contains half as much energy per litre as one litre of petrol. Two litres of fuel would need to be carried in the vehicle to give the same energy output as one litre of petrol. This is more useful than looking at enthalpy change of combustion data because it takes into account the volume of fuel that can be stored in the car. Comparing ethanol fuel to petrol gives ethanol fuel a GGE of 1.4.

2020 Paper 2Question 7 Section B · Choosing and using de-icers1 mark

Choosing and using de-icers

In some countries, winter temperatures fall below 0 °C and ice forms on roads. This causes accidents because vehicles slide on the slippery surface. De-icers are mixtures of chemical compounds that are spread on the roads to melt the ice.

The most commonly used de-icer is sodium chloride. It is used because it is very inexpensive. Calcium chloride is also used in smaller areas such as paths and car parks.

Effect of the mass of de-icer used

A scientist wanted to find out if mixtures containing a higher mass of de-icer have lower freezing points. She made solutions by adding different masses of sodium chloride to 100 cm³ samples of water at room temperature. She then measured the freezing point of each solution. She repeated the experiment with different masses of calcium chloride. Tables 7.1 and 7.2 show her results.

Table 7.1
mass of sodium chloride added/gfreezing point/°C
10-8
20-20
30-15
40does not fully dissolve
Table 7.2
mass of calcium chloride added/gfreezing point/°C
10-9
20-20
30-45
40+12

More about the chemistry of de-icers

The surface of ice has a very thin layer of water. The de-icer dissolves in this water and lowers its freezing point. This stops the water from freezing.

Some de-icers dissolve exothermically. This helps to melt the solid ice under the layer of water and allows the de-icer to work deeper in the ice.

The enthalpy change that happens during dissolving is the enthalpy change of solution, ΔHsol.

During very cold conditions, there may be very little liquid water for the de-icer to dissolve in. Some de-icers attract water vapour from the air and can use this to form a solution on the surface of the ice. De-icers that act in this way are known as hygroscopic.

2023 Paper 2Question 7 Section B · Comparing vehicle fuels (ethanol, LPG, LNG, petrol)5 marks

Comparing vehicle fuels

Car manufacturers make cars which use a range of different fuels. Some fuels are renewable, which means that they do not rely on using finite resources such as fossil fuels, and some are 'carbon neutral', which means that their use does not lead to an overall increase in the amount of carbon in the atmosphere. Other factors that need to be taken into account are the energy output of the fuel and how easy it is to store in the vehicle.

Ethanol in fuels

Ethanol fuel contains 93–96% ethanol. It is used mainly in countries such as Brazil where sugarcane can be grown in large quantities. The percentage of ethanol in the fuel is indicated by the name of the fuel. For example, E25 contains 25% ethanol by mass and E70 contains 70% ethanol by mass. In most other countries, standard petrol contains ethanol as an additive. Typically, standard petrol contains about 10% ethanol by mass and the rest is hydrocarbons. Ethanol is a useful additive to standard petrol because it increases the percentage of oxygen available for combustion.

Producing ethanol

Ethanol for use as a fuel for vehicles can be produced by either fermentation or by the catalytic addition of steam to ethene in an industrial process (see Table 7.1).

Table 7.1
processraw materialsadditional information
fermentationsugar from sugarcanereactions after fermentation produce ethanoic acid and ethyl ethanoate impurities separated by distillation or use of molecular sieves
catalytic addition of steam to etheneethene from cracking of naphtha from petroleumconditions: • 300 °C • 70 atm pressure • phosphoric(V) acid catalyst

Data about energy output

The enthalpy change of combustion is the energy given out when one mole of a pure compound burns. This can be used to compare the energy output of the main compounds in fuels, as shown in Table 7.2.

Table 7.2
type of fuelmain compoundenthalpy change of combustion of main compound in kJ/mol
LNG (liquified natural gas)methane–890
LPG (liquified petroleum gas)butane–2877
petroloctane–5470
ethanol fuelethanol–1366

Fuels are mixtures of compounds and the enthalpy change of combustion does not take into account the state or the density of the fuel.

Comparing fuels

Gaseous fuels take up a lot of storage space in a vehicle, therefore they are compressed into a liquid state. Both the mass density and the energy density (energy released per litre) of the fuels are important because they determine how far the vehicle can travel before needing to be refuelled.

Table 7.3 compares the mass density and energy density of some liquid fuels (1 L = 1000 cm³).

Table 7.3
type of fuelmass density in g/cm³energy density (energy released per litre) in kJ/L
LNG (liquified natural gas)0.4522200
LPG (liquified petroleum gas)0.5526500
petrol0.7534200
ethanol fuel0.7925000

Energy densities of fuels can be approximated by calculations which use the enthalpy change of combustion of the main compound in the fuel and the mass density of the fuel. These calculated values differ from the values shown in Table 7.3 because fuels are actually mixtures of compounds.

One way of comparing fuels is by using a GGE index. This compares the energy output of one litre of petrol to the energy output of one litre of the fuel. So, for example, a fuel with a GGE of 2.0 contains half as much energy per litre as one litre of petrol. Two litres of fuel would need to be carried in the vehicle to give the same energy output as one litre of petrol. This is more useful than looking at enthalpy change of combustion data because it takes into account the volume of fuel that can be stored in the car. Comparing ethanol fuel to petrol gives ethanol fuel a GGE of 1.4.

2024 Paper 2Question 7 Section A · Improving fuels: hydrodesulfurisation, catalytic reforming, flue gas desulfurisation2 marks

Improving Fuels

Sulfur in Crude Oil

Crude oil is separated into fractions which are further processed to make petrol and diesel fuels. Some compounds in the fractions contain sulfur. Removing the sulfur produces ultra-low sulfur petrol and diesel which produce fewer pollutants when they burn.

Hydrodesulfurisation

The sulfur is removed in a process called hydrodesulfurisation. In this process, the compounds that contain sulfur react with hydrogen. The products of the main reaction are a new carbon compound and hydrogen sulfide. The general equation for this process is shown in Equation 1.

Equation 1 R-SH + H2 → R-H + H2S (R = CnH(2n+1))

Catalytic Reforming

Some crude oil fractions are used as a feedstock for a catalytic reforming process. This process produces branched molecules or cyclic molecules from straight chain molecules. The branched molecules burn more smoothly and so are used to improve petrol. Equations 2 and 3 show examples of catalytic reforming reactions.

The catalytic reforming process involves passing heated molecules over a platinum catalyst. Sulfur compounds in the feedstock bind to the catalyst surface and make the reactions less effective. This is why hydrodesulfurisation is used to remove as much sulfur as possible from the compounds.

Flue Gas Desulfurisation

Coal and natural gas also contain sulfur compounds. The sulfur dioxide produced during combustion of these fuels in power stations is removed from the waste gases by flue gas desulfurisation. The sulfur dioxide is treated with powdered limestone. Limestone is mostly calcium carbonate with small amounts of impurities. The purity of limestone used in flue gas desulfurisation is 98%.

The reaction that takes place during the process is shown in Equation 4.

Equation 4 SO2(g) + CaCO3(s) → CaSO3(s) + CO2(g)

Nitrogen dioxide is another gas produced during combustion. Nitrogen dioxide is also removed from the waste gases by reaction with calcium carbonate in limestone. The products of the reaction between calcium carbonate and nitrogen dioxide are shown in Table 7.1.

Table 7.1
gas removedproducts of reaction with calcium carbonate
nitrogen dioxideCO2, Ca(NO3)2, Ca(NO2)2

General Equations for Reactions of Acids

Some sources, such as text books and websites, represent the general formula of an acid as HA, where A is an anion. HA can be used to give general equations for the reactions of acids.

For example, the reaction of acids with Group II metal hydroxides may be shown as:

equation 1 2HA + M(OH)2 → MA2 + 2H2O

equation 2 xHA + M → MAx + (x/2)H2

How to spot it

Common slip

2024 Paper 2Question 7 Section A · Improving fuels: hydrodesulfurisation, catalytic reforming, flue gas desulfurisation2 marks

Improving Fuels

Sulfur in Crude Oil

Crude oil is separated into fractions which are further processed to make petrol and diesel fuels. Some compounds in the fractions contain sulfur. Removing the sulfur produces ultra-low sulfur petrol and diesel which produce fewer pollutants when they burn.

Hydrodesulfurisation

The sulfur is removed in a process called hydrodesulfurisation. In this process, the compounds that contain sulfur react with hydrogen. The products of the main reaction are a new carbon compound and hydrogen sulfide. The general equation for this process is shown in Equation 1.

Equation 1 R-SH + H2 → R-H + H2S (R = CnH(2n+1))

Catalytic Reforming

Some crude oil fractions are used as a feedstock for a catalytic reforming process. This process produces branched molecules or cyclic molecules from straight chain molecules. The branched molecules burn more smoothly and so are used to improve petrol. Equations 2 and 3 show examples of catalytic reforming reactions.

The catalytic reforming process involves passing heated molecules over a platinum catalyst. Sulfur compounds in the feedstock bind to the catalyst surface and make the reactions less effective. This is why hydrodesulfurisation is used to remove as much sulfur as possible from the compounds.

Flue Gas Desulfurisation

Coal and natural gas also contain sulfur compounds. The sulfur dioxide produced during combustion of these fuels in power stations is removed from the waste gases by flue gas desulfurisation. The sulfur dioxide is treated with powdered limestone. Limestone is mostly calcium carbonate with small amounts of impurities. The purity of limestone used in flue gas desulfurisation is 98%.

The reaction that takes place during the process is shown in Equation 4.

Equation 4 SO2(g) + CaCO3(s) → CaSO3(s) + CO2(g)

Nitrogen dioxide is another gas produced during combustion. Nitrogen dioxide is also removed from the waste gases by reaction with calcium carbonate in limestone. The products of the reaction between calcium carbonate and nitrogen dioxide are shown in Table 7.1.

Table 7.1
gas removedproducts of reaction with calcium carbonate
nitrogen dioxideCO2, Ca(NO3)2, Ca(NO2)2

2022 Paper 2Question 7 Section B · Types of poly(ethene): LDPE, LLDPE, HDPE and co-polymers3 marks

Poly(ethene)

Types of poly(ethene)

The polymerisation of ethene to make poly(ethene) is usually represented as a simple addition polymerisation reaction which produces a linear chain of carbon and hydrogen atoms as shown in Fig. 7.1.

However, this is a simplified structure. In industry, different processes are used to manufacture several types of poly(ethene), each with a different structure. Fig. 7.2 shows the structures of three types of poly(ethene).

Fig. 7.3 shows another way of representing the polymer chains in each type of poly(ethene). The polymer chains shown in Fig. 7.3 are simplified representations of the real structures.

The carbon atom chains that branch out from the main polymer chain are known as side chains.

Polymerising ethene using heat and pressure results in low-density poly(ethene) (LDPE), a branched polymer. Each single LDPE molecule contains between 4000 and 40000 carbon atoms.

Co-polymers

A co-polymer is polymer that is formed from two (or more) different types of monomer.

LLDPE is made by mixing other alkenes with ethene before polymerisation. This introduces short side chains into the main polymer chain.

For example, ethene molecules can react with butene molecules to form a co-polymer. Three molecules which join to form part of a co-polymer are shown in Fig. 7.4.

The co-polymer produced has a -CH2-CH3 side chain.

World production, uses and properties of different types of poly(ethene)

Side chains push the polymer chains away from each other. In general, polymer chains with fewer side chains can be arranged closer together. This means that polymers with fewer side chains are usually more dense, less flexible, stronger and harder. The world production of each polymer differs because some types of polymer are more useful than others to make products such as building materials, packaging and hot drinks containers.

2025 Paper 2Question 7 Section A · Carbon capture storage (CCS) from methane-fuelled power stations3 marks

Carbon capture storage (CCS)

Some power stations that generate electricity use methane as a fuel. Carbon capture storage (CCS) reduces the amount of carbon dioxide entering the atmosphere. This is done by capturing carbon from methane in the form of carbon dioxide. Carbon from methane can be captured either before the methane burns (pre-combustion) or after combustion (post-combustion) as carbon dioxide.

Carbon dioxide can be stored deep underground in the space left when crude oil is extracted.

Pre-combustion capture

Steam methane reforming (SMR) and water-gas shift (WGS) are two reactions involved in pre-combustion capture of carbon from methane.

In SMR, steam reacts with methane at a pressure of 3–25 atmospheres and at a temperature of 700–1000 °C.

SMR reaction equation:

CH4 + H2O ⇌ CO + 3H2 ΔH = +206 kJ/mol

The SMR reaction is reversible and therefore the products contain small amounts of unreacted methane and water. The reaction has a percentage yield of 74%.

This is followed by the WGS reaction at 200–400 °C using a catalyst.

WGS reaction equation:

CO + H2O ⇌ CO2 + H2 ΔH = –41 kJ/mol

The carbon dioxide produced in the WGS reaction is separated from hydrogen and goes to be stored. The hydrogen is burned as a fuel to generate electricity. It does not cause environmental harm when it is combusted.

Post-combustion capture

Some power stations capture the carbon dioxide post-combustion. In order to easily separate the carbon dioxide after the reaction, the methane is burned in pure oxygen rather than air.

CH4 + 2O2 → CO2 + 2H2O

The water vapour that is produced is separated from the mixture of products. The carbon dioxide then goes to be stored.

Storing carbon dioxide

The carbon dioxide collected from the power station is pressurised. This produces liquid carbon dioxide which can then be pumped directly to be stored deep underground.

The fuel industry thinks that the space made available from the extraction of crude oil will be enough to store all the carbon dioxide produced in the world from fossil fuel combustion for many years.

2020 Paper 2Question 7 Section B · Choosing and using de-icers3 marks

Choosing and using de-icers

In some countries, winter temperatures fall below 0 °C and ice forms on roads. This causes accidents because vehicles slide on the slippery surface. De-icers are mixtures of chemical compounds that are spread on the roads to melt the ice.

The most commonly used de-icer is sodium chloride. It is used because it is very inexpensive. Calcium chloride is also used in smaller areas such as paths and car parks.

Effect of the mass of de-icer used

A scientist wanted to find out if mixtures containing a higher mass of de-icer have lower freezing points. She made solutions by adding different masses of sodium chloride to 100 cm³ samples of water at room temperature. She then measured the freezing point of each solution. She repeated the experiment with different masses of calcium chloride. Tables 7.1 and 7.2 show her results.

20-20
30-15

Table 7.2
mass of calcium chloride added/gfreezing point/°C
10-9
20-20
30-45
40+12

More about the chemistry of de-icers

The surface of ice has a very thin layer of water. The de-icer dissolves in this water and lowers its freezing point. This stops the water from freezing.

Some de-icers dissolve exothermically. This helps to melt the solid ice under the layer of water and allows the de-icer to work deeper in the ice.

The enthalpy change that happens during dissolving is the enthalpy change of solution, ΔHsol.

During very cold conditions, there may be very little liquid water for the de-icer to dissolve in. Some de-icers attract water vapour from the air and can use this to form a solution on the surface of the ice. De-icers that act in this way are known as hygroscopic.

General Equations for Reactions of Acids

Some sources, such as text books and websites, represent the general formula of an acid as HA, where A is an anion. HA can be used to give general equations for the reactions of acids.

For example, the reaction of acids with Group II metal hydroxides may be shown as:

equation 1 2HA + M(OH)2 → MA2 + 2H2O

And the reaction of acids with any metal can be shown as:

equation 2 xHA + M → MAx + (x/2)H2

where x is the value of the positive charge on the metal ion.

2024 Paper 2Question 7 Section A · Improving fuels: hydrodesulfurisation, catalytic reforming, flue gas desulfurisation2 marks

Improving Fuels

Sulfur in Crude Oil

Crude oil is separated into fractions which are further processed to make petrol and diesel fuels. Some compounds in the fractions contain sulfur. Removing the sulfur produces ultra-low sulfur petrol and diesel which produce fewer pollutants when they burn.

Hydrodesulfurisation

The sulfur is removed in a process called hydrodesulfurisation. In this process, the compounds that contain sulfur react with hydrogen. The products of the main reaction are a new carbon compound and hydrogen sulfide. The general equation for this process is shown in Equation 1.

Equation 1 R-SH + H2 → R-H + H2S (R = CnH(2n+1))

Catalytic Reforming

Some crude oil fractions are used as a feedstock for a catalytic reforming process. This process produces branched molecules or cyclic molecules from straight chain molecules. The branched molecules burn more smoothly and so are used to improve petrol. Equations 2 and 3 show examples of catalytic reforming reactions.

The catalytic reforming process involves passing heated molecules over a platinum catalyst. Sulfur compounds in the feedstock bind to the catalyst surface and make the reactions less effective. This is why hydrodesulfurisation is used to remove as much sulfur as possible from the compounds.

Flue Gas Desulfurisation

Coal and natural gas also contain sulfur compounds. The sulfur dioxide produced during combustion of these fuels in power stations is removed from the waste gases by flue gas desulfurisation. The sulfur dioxide is treated with powdered limestone. Limestone is mostly calcium carbonate with small amounts of impurities. The purity of limestone used in flue gas desulfurisation is 98%.

The reaction that takes place during the process is shown in Equation 4.

Equation 4 SO2(g) + CaCO3(s) → CaSO3(s) + CO2(g)

Nitrogen dioxide is another gas produced during combustion. Nitrogen dioxide is also removed from the waste gases by reaction with calcium carbonate in limestone. The products of the reaction between calcium carbonate and nitrogen dioxide are shown in Table 7.1.

Table 7.1
gas removedproducts of reaction with calcium carbonate
nitrogen dioxideCO2, Ca(NO3)2, Ca(NO2)2

General Equations for Reactions of Acids

Some sources, such as text books and websites, represent the general formula of an acid as HA, where A is an anion. HA can be used to give general equations for the reactions of acids.

For example, the reaction of acids with Group II metal hydroxides may be shown as:

equation 1 2HA + M(OH)2 → MA2 + 2H2O

And the reaction of acids with any metal can be shown as:

equation 2 xHA + M → MAx + (x/2)H2

where x is the value of the positive charge on the metal ion.

2022 Paper 2Question 7 Section B · Types of poly(ethene): LDPE, LLDPE, HDPE and co-polymers2 marks

Poly(ethene)

Types of poly(ethene)

The polymerisation of ethene to make poly(ethene) is usually represented as a simple addition polymerisation reaction which produces a linear chain of carbon and hydrogen atoms as shown in Fig. 7.1.

However, this is a simplified structure. In industry, different processes are used to manufacture several types of poly(ethene), each with a different structure. Fig. 7.2 shows the structures of three types of poly(ethene).

Fig. 7.3 shows another way of representing the polymer chains in each type of poly(ethene). The polymer chains shown in Fig. 7.3 are simplified representations of the real structures.

The carbon atom chains that branch out from the main polymer chain are known as side chains.

Polymerising ethene using heat and pressure results in low-density poly(ethene) (LDPE), a branched polymer. Each single LDPE molecule contains between 4000 and 40000 carbon atoms.

Co-polymers

A co-polymer is polymer that is formed from two (or more) different types of monomer.

LLDPE is made by mixing other alkenes with ethene before polymerisation. This introduces short side chains into the main polymer chain.

For example, ethene molecules can react with butene molecules to form a co-polymer. Three molecules which join to form part of a co-polymer are shown in Fig. 7.4.

The co-polymer produced has a -CH2-CH3 side chain.

World production, uses and properties of different types of poly(ethene)

Side chains push the polymer chains away from each other. In general, polymer chains with fewer side chains can be arranged closer together. This means that polymers with fewer side chains are usually more dense, less flexible, stronger and harder. The world production of each polymer differs because some types of polymer are more useful than others to make products such as building materials, packaging and hot drinks containers.

2020 Paper 2Question 7 Section B · Choosing and using de-icers4 marks

Choosing and using de-icers

In some countries, winter temperatures fall below 0 °C and ice forms on roads. This causes accidents because vehicles slide on the slippery surface. De-icers are mixtures of chemical compounds that are spread on the roads to melt the ice.

The most commonly used de-icer is sodium chloride. It is used because it is very inexpensive. Calcium chloride is also used in smaller areas such as paths and car parks.

Effect of the mass of de-icer used

A scientist wanted to find out if mixtures containing a higher mass of de-icer have lower freezing points. She made solutions by adding different masses of sodium chloride to 100 cm³ samples of water at room temperature. She then measured the freezing point of each solution. She repeated the experiment with different masses of calcium chloride. Tables 7.1 and 7.2 show her results.

Table 7.1
mass of sodium chloride added/gfreezing point/°C
10-8
20-20
30-15
40does not fully dissolve
Table 7.2
mass of calcium chloride added/gfreezing point/°C
10-9
20-20
30-45
40+12

More about the chemistry of de-icers

The surface of ice has a very thin layer of water. The de-icer dissolves in this water and lowers its freezing point. This stops the water from freezing.

Some de-icers dissolve exothermically. This helps to melt the solid ice under the layer of water and allows the de-icer to work deeper in the ice.

The enthalpy change that happens during dissolving is the enthalpy change of solution, ΔHsol.

During very cold conditions, there may be very little liquid water for the de-icer to dissolve in. Some de-icers attract water vapour from the air and can use this to form a solution on the surface of the ice. De-icers that act in this way are known as hygroscopic.

MgCl2-18-155yesspeeds up corrosion of metals, harmful to plants
KCl-4+17.2nospeeds up corrosion of metals, harmful to plants
CH4N2O (urea)-4+15.0nolow toxicity

Identify two factors that determine which de-icers are more effective at very low temperatures.

2022 Paper 2Question 7 Section B · Types of poly(ethene): LDPE, LLDPE, HDPE and co-polymers2 marks

Poly(ethene)

Types of poly(ethene)

The polymerisation of ethene to make poly(ethene) is usually represented as a simple addition polymerisation reaction which produces a linear chain of carbon and hydrogen atoms as shown in Fig. 7.1.

However, this is a simplified structure. In industry, different processes are used to manufacture several types of poly(ethene), each with a different structure. Fig. 7.2 shows the structures of three types of poly(ethene).

Fig. 7.3 shows another way of representing the polymer chains in each type of poly(ethene). The polymer chains shown in Fig. 7.3 are simplified representations of the real structures.

The carbon atom chains that branch out from the main polymer chain are known as side chains.

Polymerising ethene using heat and pressure results in low-density poly(ethene) (LDPE), a branched polymer. Each single LDPE molecule contains between 4000 and 40000 carbon atoms.

Co-polymers

A co-polymer is polymer that is formed from two (or more) different types of monomer.

LLDPE is made by mixing other alkenes with ethene before polymerisation. This introduces short side chains into the main polymer chain.

For example, ethene molecules can react with butene molecules to form a co-polymer. Three molecules which join to form part of a co-polymer are shown in Fig. 7.4.

The co-polymer produced has a -CH2-CH3 side chain.

World production, uses and properties of different types of poly(ethene)

Side chains push the polymer chains away from each other. In general, polymer chains with fewer side chains can be arranged closer together. This means that polymers with fewer side chains are usually more dense, less flexible, stronger and harder. The world production of each polymer differs because some types of polymer are more useful than others to make products such as building materials, packaging and hot drinks containers.

Table 7.1 shows information about the three polymers.

Table 7.1
type of poly(ethene)LDPELLDPEHDPE
softening temperature / °C90120130
density in g/cm³0.91–0.930.91–0.930.93–0.97
world production / millions of tonnes192438
(a)

(both are branched and contain only C and H).
Difference: LDPE has fewer, long side chains which are themselves branched;
LLDPE has many short, unbranched side chains.
[1] similarity: both branched / both have side chains on a carbon chain / same density range
[1] difference: LDPE long (branched) side chains, LLDPE short side chains
Also creditworthy as a difference: LLDPE is a co-polymer of ethene and other alkenes; LDPE is made from ethene only.

2023 Paper 2Question 7 Section B · Comparing vehicle fuels (ethanol, LPG, LNG, petrol)3 marks

Comparing vehicle fuels

Car manufacturers make cars which use a range of different fuels. Some fuels are renewable, which means that they do not rely on using finite resources such as fossil fuels, and some are 'carbon neutral', which means that their use does not lead to an overall increase in the amount of carbon in the atmosphere. Other factors that need to be taken into account are the energy output of the fuel and how easy it is to store in the vehicle.

Ethanol in fuels

Ethanol fuel contains 93–96% ethanol. It is used mainly in countries such as Brazil where sugarcane can be grown in large quantities. The percentage of ethanol in the fuel is indicated by the name of the fuel. For example, E25 contains 25% ethanol by mass and E70 contains 70% ethanol by mass. In most other countries, standard petrol contains ethanol as an additive. Typically, standard petrol contains about 10% ethanol by mass and the rest is hydrocarbons. Ethanol is a useful additive to standard petrol because it increases the percentage of oxygen available for combustion.

Producing ethanol

Ethanol for use as a fuel for vehicles can be produced by either fermentation or by the catalytic addition of steam to ethene in an industrial process (see Table 7.1).

Table 7.1
processraw materialsadditional information
fermentationsugar from sugarcanereactions after fermentation produce ethanoic acid and ethyl ethanoate impurities separated by distillation or use of molecular sieves
catalytic addition of steam to etheneethene from cracking of naphtha from petroleumconditions: • 300 °C • 70 atm pressure • phosphoric(V) acid catalyst

Data about energy output

The enthalpy change of combustion is the energy given out when one mole of a pure compound burns. This can be used to compare the energy output of the main compounds in fuels, as shown in Table 7.2.

Table 7.2
type of fuelmain compoundenthalpy change of combustion of main compound in kJ/mol
LNG (liquified natural gas)methane–890
LPG (liquified petroleum gas)butane–2877
petroloctane–5470
ethanol fuelethanol–1366

Fuels are mixtures of compounds and the enthalpy change of combustion does not take into account the state or the density of the fuel.

Comparing fuels

Gaseous fuels take up a lot of storage space in a vehicle, therefore they are compressed into a liquid state. Both the mass density and the energy density (energy released per litre) of the fuels are important because they determine how far the vehicle can travel before needing to be refuelled.

Table 7.3 compares the mass density and energy density of some liquid fuels (1 L = 1000 cm³).

Table 7.3
type of fuelmass density in g/cm³energy density (energy released per litre) in kJ/L
LNG (liquified natural gas)0.4522200
LPG (liquified petroleum gas)0.5526500
petrol0.7534200
ethanol fuel0.7925000

Energy densities of fuels can be approximated by calculations which use the enthalpy change of combustion of the main compound in the fuel and the mass density of the fuel. These calculated values differ from the values shown in Table 7.3 because fuels are actually mixtures of compounds.

One way of comparing fuels is by using a GGE index. This compares the energy output of one litre of petrol to the energy output of one litre of the fuel. So, for example, a fuel with a GGE of 2.0 contains half as much energy per litre as one litre of petrol. Two litres of fuel would need to be carried in the vehicle to give the same energy output as one litre of petrol. This is more useful than looking at enthalpy change of combustion data because it takes into account the volume of fuel that can be stored in the car. Comparing ethanol fuel to petrol gives ethanol fuel a GGE of 1.4.

[1] incorrect: ethene from crude oil (finite) / energy for heating and pressure from fossil fuels releases extra CO2

2020 Paper 2Question 7 Section B · Choosing and using de-icers1 mark

Choosing and using de-icers

In some countries, winter temperatures fall below 0 °C and ice forms on roads. This causes accidents because vehicles slide on the slippery surface. De-icers are mixtures of chemical compounds that are spread on the roads to melt the ice.

The most commonly used de-icer is sodium chloride. It is used because it is very inexpensive. Calcium chloride is also used in smaller areas such as paths and car parks.

Effect of the mass of de-icer used

A scientist wanted to find out if mixtures containing a higher mass of de-icer have lower freezing points. She made solutions by adding different masses of sodium chloride to 100 cm³ samples of water at room temperature. She then measured the freezing point of each solution. She repeated the experiment with different masses of calcium chloride. Tables 7.1 and 7.2 show her results.

Table 7.1
mass of sodium chloride added/gfreezing point/°C
10-8
20-20
30-15
40does not fully dissolve
Table 7.2
mass of calcium chloride added/gfreezing point/°C
10-9
20-20
30-45
40+12

More about the chemistry of de-icers

The surface of ice has a very thin layer of water. The de-icer dissolves in this water and lowers its freezing point. This stops the water from freezing.

Some de-icers dissolve exothermically. This helps to melt the solid ice under the layer of water and allows the de-icer to work deeper in the ice.

The enthalpy change that happens during dissolving is the enthalpy change of solution, ΔHsol.

During very cold conditions, there may be very little liquid water for the de-icer to dissolve in. Some de-icers attract water vapour from the air and can use this to form a solution on the surface of the ice. De-icers that act in this way are known as hygroscopic.

are drawn about as large as C (0.077 nm). The sticks are not to scale:
bond length ≈ sum of radii, so atoms are touching, not far apart.
[1] dot-and-cross is 2D / does not show shape, bond lengths or atom sizes
[1] ball and stick: relative sizes of atoms wrong (H drawn too large)
[1] ball and stick: bond lengths not to scale / atoms should touch (overlap)
Accept: ball and stick model does not show electrons / lone pairs on O.

2025 Paper 2Question 7 Section A · Carbon capture storage (CCS) from methane-fuelled power stations1 mark

Carbon capture storage (CCS)

Some power stations that generate electricity use methane as a fuel. Carbon capture storage (CCS) reduces the amount of carbon dioxide entering the atmosphere. This is done by capturing carbon from methane in the form of carbon dioxide. Carbon from methane can be captured either before the methane burns (pre-combustion) or after combustion (post-combustion) as carbon dioxide.

Carbon dioxide can be stored deep underground in the space left when crude oil is extracted.

Pre-combustion capture

Steam methane reforming (SMR) and water-gas shift (WGS) are two reactions involved in pre-combustion capture of carbon from methane.

In SMR, steam reacts with methane at a pressure of 3–25 atmospheres and at a temperature of 700–1000 °C.

SMR reaction equation:

CH4 + H2O ⇌ CO + 3H2 ΔH = +206 kJ/mol

The SMR reaction is reversible and therefore the products contain small amounts of unreacted methane and water. The reaction has a percentage yield of 74%.

This is followed by the WGS reaction at 200–400 °C using a catalyst.

WGS reaction equation:

CO + H2O ⇌ CO2 + H2 ΔH = –41 kJ/mol

The carbon dioxide produced in the WGS reaction is separated from hydrogen and goes to be stored. The hydrogen is burned as a fuel to generate electricity. It does not cause environmental harm when it is combusted.

Post-combustion capture

Some power stations capture the carbon dioxide post-combustion. In order to easily separate the carbon dioxide after the reaction, the methane is burned in pure oxygen rather than air.

CH4 + 2O2 → CO2 + 2H2O

The water vapour that is produced is separated from the mixture of products. The carbon dioxide then goes to be stored.

Storing carbon dioxide

The carbon dioxide collected from the power station is pressurised. This produces liquid carbon dioxide which can then be pumped directly to be stored deep underground.

The fuel industry thinks that the space made available from the extraction of crude oil will be enough to store all the carbon dioxide produced in the world from fossil fuel combustion for many years.

(d)(i)

Suggest how carbon dioxide is separated from the mixture of combustion products in the post-combustion capture process.

2025 · Q7(d)(i)[1]
Cool the mixture so that the water vapour condenses to liquid water;
the carbon dioxide remains a gas and is collected.
[1] cool / condense the water vapour (CO2 stays as gas)
